about: Long labelled memory pairs (content 1,000-4,000 characters each) for checking duplicate detection on long memories; classes as in similarity-pairs.json. Classes that must be flagged: same (one rule restated with other examples and wording). Reviewed together as overlaps: exception (a global rule and its narrower project or situation exception). Not to be grouped as duplicates: unrelated (different rules in one category group that share vocabulary).

a.content: Never push, publish, tag or deploy without the user's explicit go-ahead for that specific action. A push to main deploys production in several of the user's repositories, so a push is never a harmless step that can be undone later. Before pushing, say what will be pushed (the branch, the commits by subject line, and whether it is a fast-forward), where it goes (which remote), and what it triggers (a deploy, a release workflow, a docs build), then wait for a clear yes in chat. Approval for one push does not carry over to the next push, to a tag, or to a publish: each is asked for on its own, even within the same session and the same task. A yes given for "push the fix" does not cover tagging the release afterwards, and a yes for a dry run does not cover the real run. When a script would push as a side effect (a release helper, a deploy recipe, a git hook that pushes tags), treat running the script as the push and ask first. If a project memory grants that project a standing exception (for example, pushing feature branches to a personal fork is fine), follow the exception exactly as stated and nothing beyond it. Registry writes are never done by the agent at all: npm publish, cargo publish, dist-tag changes, release-workflow dispatches and tag pushes are prepared and then handed to the user to run. Creating anything on the user's hosted accounts, such as a repository, a gist, a release or a fork, also needs the plan described and approved first. If unsure whether an action counts as publishing, assume it does and ask. Worked examples of what needs its own yes: the user approves "push the fix to my fork", and the agent then notices a version bump is due; the bump, the tag and the release are three new questions. A CI job that deploys on every push to main makes even a one-line documentation fix a deployment. A just recipe called release that builds, tags and uploads is run only after the user has approved the release as a whole and seen what it will do. Opening a pull request on a project the user owns is governed by that project's own rule; on someone else's project it is a contribution that needs the user's yes and follows the upstream contribution rules. When the user is away, prepared work waits in a local branch with a short note of the exact command that would publish it, rather than being pushed so that it is ready. Pushing a branch to back it up is still a push. Why the rule is strict: in the user's projects a push can start a production deploy, publish a docs site to the public, release a container image that servers pull automatically, or notify subscribers of a new version, and none of these can be quietly taken back once seen. A force push can also destroy a collaborator's commits on a shared branch. So the agent prepares everything up to the irreversible step and then stops: the branch is rebased and tested, the changelog entry is written, the version is bumped in a local commit, and the exact commands that would publish are written into the reply. The user then runs them or says yes to each. If the user says "ship it" without naming the steps, ask which steps they mean before doing any of them, listing them in order. If a push is rejected because the remote moved, do not resolve it by force pushing; fetch, look at what changed, and ask. After an approved push, report the resulting commit range and any job it triggered, with links, so the user can follow it. When a CI pipeline that runs after the push fails, say so and propose a fix, but do not push the fix without asking again. Tags are especially sensitive because release tooling often treats a pushed tag as the instruction to publish, so a tag is never created on a commit the user has not reviewed, and never moved once pushed.

b.content: Ask before every push, publish, tag or deployment, and wait for an explicit yes. Pushing to main ships to production in some of the user's projects, so an agent must never treat git push as routine. When the work is ready, describe the outgoing change first: the local branch and target remote, the list of commits with their subjects, and anything the push sets off, such as a CI deploy, a package release or a site rebuild. Only push after the user says yes for that push. A yes is good for that one action only: it does not extend to a later push in the same conversation, to creating or pushing a tag, to publishing a package, or to dispatching a release workflow, which each get their own question. Running a helper that pushes or tags as part of its job counts the same as pushing by hand, so ask before running it. Some repositories have a written standing exception in their project memory, for instance that work-in-progress branches may be pushed to the user's own fork without asking; such an exception applies only in that repository and only to what it says. The agent never writes to a package registry itself (no cargo publish, no npm publish, no dist-tag), and never creates repositories, releases, gists or forks on the user's accounts without first laying out the plan and getting approval. When it is unclear whether something publishes, ask rather than guess. Some cases that each need a separate question: after a yes for pushing a branch, tagging that branch is a new action; a deploy triggered automatically by a merge to main makes the merge itself something to ask about; a make or just target that wraps git push --tags is run only once the user has seen and approved what it publishes. Pull requests follow the project's own rule when the user owns it, and the upstream contribution rules otherwise. While the user is away, finished work stays local with the exact publishing command written down for them, instead of being pushed ahead of time. A push made only to keep a backup of the branch is still a push and is asked for too. The reasoning behind it: a single push may deploy the production service, put a documentation change live, build and publish an image that machines fetch on their own, or announce a version to everyone watching the repository, and those effects cannot be recalled. Force pushing to a shared branch can also wipe out other people's work. The agent therefore does all of the preparation and halts just before the irreversible step: tests pass, the branch is up to date, release notes are drafted, the version change sits in a local commit, and the reply shows the precise commands that would publish. The user either runs them or approves them one by one. A vague "go ahead and release" is answered with the list of steps it would involve, asking which ones are meant. A rejected push because the remote has new commits is resolved by fetching and asking, never by forcing. After a push the user approved, share the commit range and links to the jobs it started. If CI then fails, report it with a proposed fix, and ask before pushing that fix too. Treat tags with extra care, since release automation commonly publishes on a new tag: tag only commits the user has reviewed, and never move a tag after it has been pushed.

a.content: In Rust, a panic is reserved for a broken invariant, a state the code itself guarantees cannot happen. It is never the answer to an expected failure: input/output errors, a missing or unreadable file, bad user input, a malformed configuration, a network error or a timeout are all returned as a Result and propagated with the question-mark operator, with context added where it helps the reader of the error (which file, which setting, which id). Outside tests there is no unwrap at all. Where an expect is genuinely needed, its message names the invariant that makes the failure unreachable, for example expect("the regex is a literal checked by a test"), not expect("failed") or expect("should work"). Prefer constructs that make the panic impossible instead of asserting it away: let-else to bail out of an Option early, the ? operator, infallible conversions such as From instead of TryFrom plus unwrap, iterators instead of indexing when the index might be out of range, and types that cannot represent the invalid state. Library code never calls process::exit or prints to stdout to report an error; it returns the error and lets the binary decide. Tests are the exception: unwrap and expect are fine in tests and test helpers, because a panic there is exactly the failure report wanted. When reviewing code, treat a new unwrap outside tests as a defect to fix, not a style nit. Concrete patterns: config loading returns Result<Config> with the path in the error context; a CLI argument that fails to parse is reported through clap's error, not a panic; a lookup that may miss returns Option and the caller decides; array access inside a loop whose bounds are computed is replaced by iteration or get(). In async code the same rules hold, and a JoinError is mapped to an error rather than unwrapped. A panic in a tool handler of a long-running server is especially bad, since it ends the request without a reply, so servers return errors and log them instead.

b.content: Rust error handling: expected failures are values, not panics. Reading a file that may be missing, parsing a user's argument, opening a database, calling an HTTP endpoint that can time out, or decoding a config file that may be malformed all return Result, and callers use ? to pass the error up with added context naming what was being done. Panics are only for violated invariants that the program's own logic rules out. Production code contains no unwrap. An expect is acceptable only with a message stating the invariant, e.g. expect("checked non-empty two lines above"); vague messages like expect("oops") are not acceptable. Better still, write the code so the invariant is enforced by the compiler or by structure: use let-else for early returns on None, use From conversions that cannot fail, iterate instead of indexing, and choose types that make invalid states unrepresentable. A library function never exits the process or prints its own errors; it hands the error back to the caller and the binary formats it once. In tests the rules relax completely: unwrap and expect are the normal way to fail a test, inside test functions and their helpers alike. In review, an unwrap added to non-test code is a bug to fix before merging. Typical cases: opening the store returns an error naming the store path; an unknown subcommand argument is a clap error; a map lookup that can miss yields Option; computed indices are replaced by get() or iterators. In async code a failed join is turned into an error, never unwrapped. Long-running servers must never panic inside a request handler, because the request then ends with no reply at all and the client hangs; they return the error to the client instead.

a.content: Write user-facing text in plain, direct English without filler, flattery or hedging. Lead with the answer or the result, then give only the detail the reader needs to act on it; offer more on request instead of piling it on. Avoid stock openers such as "Great question", "Certainly" or "I'd be happy to", and closers such as "Let me know if you need anything else". Prefer short sentences and common words: "use" rather than "utilize", "help" rather than "facilitate", "start" rather than "commence". Do not soften statements with "it seems", "it might be worth considering" or "perhaps" when the facts are known; say what is true and how sure you are, once. Use the user's own terms for their project, and define a technical term the first time it appears if the reader may not know it. Keep formatting light: headings and bullet lists when they make a long answer easier to scan, never for two or three sentences. Numbers, names, commands and error messages are given exactly. When something failed, say so plainly with the evidence, and say what was not done or not checked. These rules hold for chat replies, commit messages, pull request descriptions, documentation and code comments alike.

b.content: Keep the prose plain and to the point, in every place the user reads it: replies, docs, commit messages, PR bodies and comments. Put the conclusion first and follow it with what the reader needs to act, nothing more; further detail is for when they ask. Cut ceremony: no "Absolutely!", no "Happy to help", no "Hope this helps", no praise of the question. Choose everyday words over inflated ones, so "use" instead of "leverage", "show" instead of "demonstrate", "end" instead of "terminate". Don't hedge facts you have verified with phrases like "it appears that" or "you may want to consider"; state them and give the confidence level once if it matters. Match the vocabulary the user already uses for their codebase, and explain jargon at first use when the reader might not know it. Formatting should help scanning, not decorate: use lists and headings for long answers only. Quote commands, paths, versions and error text exactly as they are. If a step failed or was skipped, say that directly and show the output that proves it, rather than burying it.

a.content: Every behaviour change ships with a test, and every bug fix ships with a test that fails without the fix. Before trusting a new test, make it fail once on purpose: revert the fix, or break the code it covers, and watch the test turn red with the expected message; a test that has never failed may not be testing anything. Prefer extending or parametrising an existing test when the new case exercises the same path; add a new test only when it catches a failure that no existing case catches. Tests assert on observable behaviour (outputs, stored rows, files, exit codes, error messages), not on private implementation details that a refactor would change. Keep tests deterministic: no sleeping for timing, no dependence on the clock, network or the user's real home directory; use temporary directories and fixed inputs. When a test is flaky, fix the cause rather than adding a retry. Mutation testing is a good check of a suite's strength on risky code: surviving mutants are either covered with a new assertion or documented as equivalent with the reason. For example, a fix for a migration that dropped rows ships with a test that builds the old store, runs the migration and compares every row, and the commit says the test failed before the fix with the exact message.

b.content: New behaviour needs a test, and a fix for a bug needs a regression test that would have failed before the fix. Prove each new test can fail: undo the change or sabotage the code under test and confirm the test reports the failure you expect; never rely on a test that has only ever passed. When a new case runs through the same code as an existing test, add it to that test (a table of cases, or a parameter) instead of writing another function; a separate test is justified only by a failure mode nothing else detects. Check behaviour the user can observe, such as command output, exit status, database contents, written files and error text, rather than internals that would break the test on a harmless refactor. Tests must be repeatable: avoid sleeps and wall-clock assumptions, external services and the real home directory, and work in throwaway directories with fixed data. A flaky test is a bug to diagnose, never something to paper over with retries. For high-risk code, run mutation testing and either kill each surviving mutant with a better assertion or record why it is equivalent. For instance, a fix to a parser that rejected a valid file comes with that file as a fixture and a test that parsed it with the old code and failed; the commit mentions the failure seen before the fix.

a.content: Nothing in a public repository, its releases, its CI configuration or its published artefacts may reveal or grant access to the user's private infrastructure or personal details. That rules out committing or publishing API keys, tokens, webhook secrets, SSH keys, passwords, private host names, internal IP addresses and ports, container registry hosts, VPN names, or paths and usernames from the user's own machines baked into scripts, docs or binaries. Example configuration uses obviously fake placeholders (example.invalid, 192.0.2.10, <token>) rather than real values with a few characters changed. Server configuration for the user's own machines lives in private repositories, never in the public project, even when it would be convenient to keep it next to the code. Before every commit and release, scan the diff and the release assets for such strings; a leaked secret is rotated immediately, and history is rewritten only with the user's agreement. CI logs count as published: never echo secrets or private hosts in build steps. The rule also covers screenshots, recordings and logs attached to issues or releases: crop or redact them.

b.content: Keep the user's private infrastructure and personal data out of everything public: the repository contents and history, release notes and assets, CI workflows and their logs, packages and container images. Do not commit or ship secrets of any kind (API keys, access tokens, SSH or signing keys, webhook secrets, passwords), nor details that point to the user's own setup, such as private host names, LAN addresses, ports, registry domains, local file-system paths or usernames embedded in scripts, docs or compiled artefacts. Examples and templates use clearly invented values like example.invalid or documentation-range addresses, not slightly altered real ones. Deployment and server configuration for the user's machines belong in a private repository, separate from the public code. Review each diff and every release artefact for these strings before committing or publishing. If a secret does leak, rotate it at once; rewriting history needs the user's say-so. Treat CI output as public and never print secrets or internal hosts there. Screenshots, terminal recordings and log excerpts attached anywhere public are redacted the same way.

a.content: Rebase feature branches onto the target branch instead of merging the target branch into them, and land them as a linear history. Before opening or updating a pull request, rebase onto the latest base branch so the branch contains only its own commits, in order, each of which builds and passes the tests on its own. Squash fixup commits into the commit they fix before review rather than leaving "fix typo" and "address review" commits in the history; interactive rebasing is done by the user or with an autosquash command, never by rewriting someone else's pushed commits. Merge commits are avoided because they bury the change's own commits under the base branch's history and make bisecting harder. Conflicts are resolved during the rebase, one commit at a time, and the result is re-tested. After a rebase, a pushed branch needs a force push, which is done with --force-with-lease and only on the agent's own feature branch, never on main or a shared branch. When a rebase goes wrong, abort it and start again from the reflog entry rather than piling fixes on top. Long-lived branches are rebased often so conflicts stay small. Before force pushing, compare the branch with its remote copy to make sure nobody else pushed to it in the meantime. A pull request's description keeps a short list of what changed between review rounds, since rebasing hides the per-round diff. Example sequence: git fetch origin, git rebase origin/main, run the tests, git push --force-with-lease, then note in the pull request that it was rebased. If the base branch moved under an open review, rebase only after the reviewer has finished the current round, so their comments stay attached to the lines they were written on. Release branches are never rebased once a release has been cut from them; fixes are cherry-picked onto them instead. Why the user prefers this: a linear history reads like a story of the project, git log --oneline shows one line per change, git bisect lands on the commit that introduced a bug instead of a merge, and reverting a change means reverting one commit. Rebasing also forces conflicts to be resolved by the person who knows the change best, at the time they write it, rather than in a merge commit nobody reviews. Squash-merging through the hosting service is acceptable when a branch's commits are not individually meaningful, but well-structured commits are preferred over a single squashed one, because each commit's message explains one decision. When a branch depends on another open branch, rebase it onto that branch and retarget the pull request once the first one merges. Rebased branches are checked once more after the rebase with the full test command, not only the tests near the conflict, because a clean textual rebase can still combine two changes that do not work together.

b.content: In the company monorepo the user works on (github.com/acme/platform), every pull request must be merged with a merge commit; rebasing feature branches and squash merging are both disabled by the repository's settings, and the release tooling reads merge commits to build the changelog. So in that repository only: do not rebase a branch that has been pushed, do not force push, and bring the base branch in with git merge when the branch falls behind. Keep the branch's own commits readable anyway, since the merge commit lists them in the changelog: one logical change per commit, with a subject that would make sense in release notes. Fixup commits are acceptable there, because the history is never rewritten after pushing, but say in the commit body which earlier commit they fix. This exception exists because the team's release process depends on it; everywhere else the user's general preference for rebasing applies. The release bot fails loudly when it finds a branch whose history was rewritten after review, and the team has asked contributors more than once not to force push to shared branches, so treat a force push in this repository as something that needs the user's explicit approval even on a personal branch. To keep that history useful, write merge commit messages that summarise the branch in one line. Pull the base branch in only when there is a reason (a conflict, a needed fix), not on every push, so the branch does not fill with merges of main. Old branches that were rebased in the past before this rule existed stay as they are. The team's tooling also links each merge commit to the pull request number in the changelog, so the merge commit subject keeps the hosting service's default form (Merge pull request #123 from owner/branch) rather than a custom one, and the pull request title becomes the changelog line: write it in the past-tense style the changelog uses. Reviews in that repository happen on the pull request as a whole, so there is no need to restructure the commits for review, but avoid committing work-in-progress snapshots with meaningless messages, because they still appear in the changelog's commit list. If a branch's history becomes hard to read, close the pull request and open a fresh one from a new branch with a cleaner history, rather than rewriting the pushed branch.

a.content: Do not add new dependencies without asking the user first. A new crate, npm package or Python library brings maintenance, security review, licence questions and build time, so propose it with the reason, the alternatives considered (including writing the few lines needed by hand or using the standard library), the package's maintenance state and licence, and its transitive dependency count, then wait for approval. Upgrading an existing dependency within its current major version for a fix is fine without asking, but say so in the commit message; a major-version upgrade needs approval like a new dependency. Development-only tools follow the same rule when they are added to the project's lockfile. Prefer small, widely used, well-maintained packages over clever ones, and never vendor code from a package without its licence. Typical alternatives to a new dependency: the standard library's own types, a short helper function with a test, or a feature of a dependency the project already has. When asking, show the size of the package and the number of maintainers, its release cadence over the last year, any open security advisories, and whether its licence is compatible with the project's. If the user declines, implement the small piece by hand and say what was given up.

b.content: For the user-memory project specifically, test-only dependencies may be added without asking, as long as they go under dev-dependencies and are small and well maintained: tempfile, assert_cmd, predicates and similar crates that make integration tests clearer. The user agreed to this because the test suite grows quickly and asking for every helper crate slows the work down without adding safety, since dev-dependencies never reach the shipped binary. Say in the commit message which test dependency was added and why. Runtime dependencies in that project still need approval, exactly as everywhere else, and so do build-dependencies and anything that changes what is compiled into the release binary. If a test dependency pulls in a large tree (more than a handful of transitive crates), ask first anyway. The same applies to test fixtures copied from other projects: they may be added freely if their licence allows it and the source is named in the fixture's header comment. Examples of test helpers that fit: tempfile for scratch directories, a small JSON assertion helper, or a property-testing crate for a parser. A mocking framework that rewrites the code under test does not fit, because it changes how the shipped code is structured.

a.content: Write all code comments, commit messages, documentation and pull request text in English, whatever language the conversation is in. The user's projects are public or may become public, and English keeps them readable to any contributor and consistent with the ecosystem's tooling and error messages. Identifiers follow English naming as well. Chat replies follow the language the user writes in, but anything that lands in a repository is English. When translating the user's wording into a commit message or comment, keep the meaning exact rather than paraphrasing loosely, and keep product names and technical terms as the project spells them. Use American or British spelling consistently within one project, matching what the project already uses. Quoted error messages, log output and command lines are reproduced exactly as they appear, even when they contain words in another language, because changing them would make them impossible to search for. Documentation examples, sample configuration files and test fixtures with prose follow the same rule.

b.content: In the user's Spanish-language community project (the documentation site for a regional Python user group), documentation pages and the README are written in Spanish, because the audience reads Spanish first and several members asked for it. Code comments and commit messages in that repository stay in English like everywhere else, so the code remains readable to outside contributors and the commit history matches the rest of the user's work. When editing a documentation page there, keep the existing Spanish terms the members already use for Python concepts, and do not mix English sentences into Spanish paragraphs except for code, command names and error text. If unsure of a Spanish technical term, keep the English term in italics rather than inventing a translation, and mention it to the user so a native speaker can decide. Pull request descriptions there may be in either language; follow the language of the issue being fixed. Images with text, such as diagrams and screenshots, use Spanish labels on those documentation pages.

a.content: Leave no stale branches or worktrees behind. When a branch's pull request is merged or closed, remove its worktree, delete the local branch, and delete the remote branch if the hosting service did not already. Before removing anything, check that the worktree has no uncommitted changes and that its commits landed upstream, comparing by patch id rather than commit hash, because squash and rebase merges change hashes. Clean up when finishing a task, then run git worktree prune. Never remove a worktree or branch that belongs to another task or another person, even if it looks abandoned; ask instead. Worktrees go in one folder beside the checkouts, <worktrees>/<project>/<name>, so they are easy to find and remove, never inside the main checkout. Exceptions are rare and are written down: a worktree may be kept while its pull request is still open, or while the user has asked to keep it for comparison. Before deleting a remote branch, check that no other open pull request is based on it. Stale worktrees found from earlier tasks are listed to the user, not removed silently. A typical cleanup at the end of a task: git -C <worktree> status to confirm it is clean, git cherry or a patch-id comparison to confirm the commits landed, git worktree remove <path>, git branch -d <branch>, git push origin --delete <branch> when the remote copy remains, and finally git worktree prune.

b.content: An automation bot that the user runs across several rounds of work in one project may keep its own standing worktree instead of removing it after each task: between rounds it resets that worktree to the new base branch rather than deleting and recreating it, because the user set the bot up with that path and other tools point at it. The worktree goes only when the user retires that bot. This is a narrow exception to cleaning up after every task: branches created for individual pull requests inside that standing worktree are still deleted locally and remotely once their pull request is merged or closed, after the same patch-id check that their commits landed. The standing worktree itself must still be clean (no uncommitted changes, no stray untracked files) at the end of every round, so that the reset to the new base cannot lose work. Example: a nightly dependency-update bot keeps <worktrees>/<project>/dependency-bot for as long as it runs, and at the start of each round runs git fetch, then resets the worktree to the new base after confirming it is clean. Branches it created for fixes in earlier rounds are removed once merged. If the reset would discard anything, the bot stops and asks.

a.content: Keep a security finding out of issues, pull requests, commit messages, changesets and release notes until the maintainer has decided how to handle it. Report it privately, through the project's security contact or the private channel the user names, with a reproduction that proves the issue and its impact, and without publishing an exploit. When a fix lands before a disclosure plan exists, describe the change neutrally (what it fixes in behaviour, not how to attack it) and avoid words that point attackers at the weakness, such as "bypass", "injection" or "exploit". Never test a suspected vulnerability against systems the user does not own or have permission to test. Credentials found during the work are reported to the user privately and never copied into notes, logs or memory. If the user asks for a public write-up later, it is drafted privately first and shared only after the maintainer agrees. A proof of concept is kept minimal and local, never pushed to a public repository or gist. When the finding concerns a third-party dependency, the report goes to that dependency's maintainers privately, and the user's own project waits for their fix or an agreed date before saying anything public.

b.content: For vulnerabilities the user reports in their own unpublished side project (a note-taking tool, not yet released to anyone), the private-disclosure process is not needed: there are no users to protect yet, so the finding may be described plainly in the fix's commit message and pull request, including how it could be abused, which helps future reviewers understand why the code is written the way it is. This applies only while the project has no published release and no other users; from the first public release on, the general rule of keeping findings private until the maintainer decides applies again. Secrets found in that project are still never written into commits, logs or memory, and testing still stays on the user's own machines and test stores, never on real data. Example: a path traversal found in the export command before the first release can be fixed in a commit titled fix(export): refuse file names that leave the exports folder, with a body explaining the attack and the test that proves it. After the first release, the same finding would be reported privately first.

a.content: In Rust, model domain states with enums and newtypes so invalid states cannot be represented: an email address is an Email newtype validated once at construction, a memory's status is an enum rather than a string compared in five places, and an id is a Uuid rather than a String. Parse at the boundary and pass typed values inward, so functions deep in the code never re-validate input. Prefer exhaustive match over if-else chains on enums, so adding a variant makes the compiler point at every place that must handle it. Avoid boolean parameters whose meaning is unclear at the call site; use a two-variant enum with descriptive names instead. Keep structs' fields private when an invariant ties them together, and expose constructors that uphold it. Derive Debug for every public type, and implement Display only for types whose text a user reads, such as error messages and identifiers printed by the CLI. For example, parse command-line flags into a Settings struct with typed fields once in main, and pass &Settings down; functions then take a Timeout or a Url rather than raw strings and numbers. Converting between the typed values and their wire format happens in one module per format. When a function would take more than three or four parameters of the same primitive type, introduce a small struct so call sites name each value. More examples of the same idea: a duration read from configuration becomes a std::time::Duration at the edge rather than a number of milliseconds passed around; a file path that must exist is checked once and carried as a PathBuf that is known to be valid for the operation, with the check's error naming the path; a schema version is an integer newtype with a comparison that knows which versions can be migrated. State machines are enums whose variants carry only the data valid in that state, so a connection that is not yet authenticated simply has no token field to read by mistake. Builders are used for structs with many optional fields, with the required ones as arguments to the builder's constructor, so forgetting one is a compile error rather than a runtime default. Avoid stringly-typed maps for structured data that has a known shape: define a struct and derive serde for it, so a typo in a field name fails to compile instead of silently reading nothing.

b.content: In Rust code, write documentation comments on every public item explaining why it exists and when to use it, not restating its signature: a doc comment on a function says what the caller can rely on, which errors it returns and in which situations, and any panics with the invariant behind them. Module-level docs (//! at the top of a file) give the overview a newcomer needs to find their way: what the module owns, what it deliberately does not do, and where related code lives. Private helpers get a short comment only when the reason for the code is not obvious from the code itself. Keep examples in doc comments compiling by running cargo test --doc, and prefer a short runnable example over a long prose description. When behaviour changes, update the comments in the same commit, so a comment never describes code that no longer exists. Comments in tests explain the scenario being exercised and why the expected outcome is right, since a test is often the first place someone looks when it fails. Example: a function that opens the store documents that it creates the file when missing, returns an error naming the path when it cannot be opened, and never runs migrations, pointing to the function that does. A module doc for the search code lists the two signals it combines and where each is calibrated. Comments that only repeat the code, such as // increment i, are removed during review. More guidance for comments: a doc comment's first sentence is a short summary that reads well in the generated documentation's index, followed by details in later paragraphs. Use intra-doc links, such as [`connect`], to point at related items so the links stay correct when items move. Unsafe blocks always carry a // SAFETY: comment stating why each requirement of the unsafe operation is met. Constants get a comment that justifies their value, including where it was measured or which specification it comes from, because a bare number invites someone to change it. TODO comments name what is missing and why it is not done yet; a TODO without a reason is either done now or removed. Comments are kept in the same language and tone as the rest of the codebase, and long explanations that apply to a whole module move into the module's top-level documentation rather than being repeated at each use.

a.content: Commit messages follow Conventional Commits: a type (feat, fix, refactor, docs, test, chore, perf, build, ci), an optional scope naming one area of the code, and a subject in the imperative mood under about 72 characters, with no trailing period. One commit holds one logical change with its tests and docs. The body, wrapped at 72 columns, explains why the change was made and what it means for users, not a line-by-line list of what changed, which the diff already shows. Reference issues in the body or footer. Breaking changes get an exclamation mark after the type and a BREAKING CHANGE footer describing the migration. No attribution lines, tool names or co-author trailers for automated helpers: the human submitter is the sole author. Example subjects: fix(store): never open the store file outside SQLite once it exists; docs: describe the repair command; refactor(index): share the keyword refill. A change that needs two scopes is usually two commits. Merge commits created by the hosting service keep its default message. Revert commits use git revert and explain in the body why the change is reverted and what replaces it, if anything.

b.content: Keep the git history of the user's repositories free of large binary files and generated output. Build artefacts, coverage reports, local databases, editor and OS files (such as .DS_Store), downloaded archives and vendored dependency caches stay out of commits; the .gitignore lists them, and a pre-commit hook may block known patterns. Test fixtures are committed only when small and needed by the tests, and generated fixtures are produced by a documented command rather than edited by hand. If a large file was committed by mistake and not yet pushed, remove it from the commit before pushing; once pushed, ask the user before rewriting history. Images for documentation are compressed and kept under a docs/assets folder, and anything over a few megabytes goes to the release assets instead of the repository. Lockfiles are always committed for applications and binaries, so builds are reproducible, and kept in sync with the manifest in the same commit that changes a dependency. Before committing, run git status and git diff --stat to see every file being added, and check the size of any new file over a hundred kilobytes.

a.content: Integration tests for command-line tools run the real compiled binary as a subprocess, with HOME, configuration directories and data paths pointed at a temporary directory, so they can never read or modify the user's real files. Each test creates its own temporary directory and does not depend on the order in which tests run or on state left by another test. Environment variables that could leak in from the developer's shell (tokens, URLs, paths) are removed explicitly in the test's command builder. Output is asserted on exact strings for messages users rely on, and parsed as JSON where the command prints JSON. Tests that need an external service, such as an embedding model, skip themselves cleanly when the service is not configured, and say how to run them. Slow tests are not marked ignored to make the suite faster; instead the slow part is made faster or the case is moved to a unit test of the function that matters. Example: a test for the setup command sets HOME, CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and CODEX_HOME to subfolders of a tempdir, removes USER_MEMORY_URL and USER_MEMORY_TOKEN_FILE from the environment, runs the binary, and then checks the files it wrote under the tempdir.

b.content: When a test fails, investigate before changing the test: read the failure output in full, reproduce it on its own, and find out whether the code or the test is wrong. Never change an expected value to whatever the code now returns without understanding why it changed, and never delete or ignore a failing test to get a green run. If the test expectation was genuinely wrong, say so in the commit that fixes it, with the reason. When a failure only happens sometimes, record the seed, the timing or the environment that triggers it, and fix the race or the shared state rather than adding retries. Report test results honestly: the exact command, the pass and fail counts, and which tests did not run, including those skipped for missing services. A suite that passes only after re-running is reported as flaky, with the failing run's output attached, not as passing. Example: a test that fails one run in twenty because two threads write the same temporary file is fixed by giving each write its own file name, and the commit explains the race; it is not fixed by retrying.

a.content: Before starting work in a repository, read its own instructions first: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and the README's development section, plus any docs they point to. Follow the project's conventions over general habits: its task runner (just, make, npm scripts) rather than raw commands, its formatting and lint settings, its test commands and its branch and commit rules. When the project's rules conflict with the user's general preferences, the project's written rules win for that repository, and the conflict is mentioned to the user once. If a project has no instructions, look at recent commits and existing code for the conventions in use, and match them. Re-read the instructions after a long break in a session, since they may have changed on the main branch in the meantime. Examples: run the project's just check rather than cargo test directly when it exists, honour a CONTRIBUTING.md rule that every change needs a changelog entry, and keep to an AGENTS.md rule that plans live outside the repository. If the instructions name a commit hook path, keep the setting as it is.

b.content: When a task is long or touches several areas, keep a short written plan and update it as the work progresses: the steps in order, which one is in progress, and what is done. Plans and progress notes live outside the repository (for example in a temporary folder), never as committed files, unless the project explicitly keeps design documents in its docs folder. Break the work so each step ends in a state that builds and passes its tests, and commit at those points. If the plan changes because something unexpected turned up, say what changed and why before continuing. At the end, summarise what was done, what was verified and how, and what was not done or not checked. A step that turns out to need a decision from the user stops the plan there, with the question asked plainly and the options laid out. Example: a plan for a schema change lists the migration step, its test, the snapshot, the docs, and the verification commands, each marked done as it completes, in a file under /tmp that is never committed.

a.content: When reporting the results of a review, list findings ranked by severity, each with the file and line, a one-sentence statement of the defect, and the concrete scenario that triggers it: the input, the state, and the wrong output or crash it produces. Separate verified findings from suspicions, and say how each was verified (a test run, a probe, a reading of the code). Group minor style points at the end, or leave them out if they do not change meaning. Do not pad a review with praise or with restatements of what the code does; the author knows. End with what was not reviewed or not checked, so the reader knows the limits of the review. When a finding comes with a suggested fix, keep the suggestion short and mark it as optional unless the fix is the only safe option. Example entry: High: src/store.rs:42 drops locks on close; two writers then corrupt the index (probe: two servers, 160 writes each, integrity_check fails 5 of 5); fix: open the file through SQLite only. Mark the severity scale used, so the reader can compare reviews.

b.content: When the user asks a question about how something works, answer with the explanation they need at their level, using their own code or setup as the example rather than a generic one. Start from what they already know (their project, the tools they named) and build only as far as the question requires. Use a small concrete example, such as the exact command, a three-line snippet or a short table of inputs and outputs, before any abstract description. If the honest answer depends on something not yet known, say what it depends on and how to find out. Offer to go deeper at the end in one short line instead of writing the deeper explanation up front. Avoid diagrams and long analogies unless the user asks for them; a precise sentence usually serves better. Example: asked why a test is slow, show the one line that waits on a timeout and the measured time, then say how to shorten it, rather than describing the test framework in general. Keep the answer's first sentence a direct answer to the question asked.
